The outer loop starts with i := 1, so the invariant `i <= a.Length` (line 35) must hold on entry, which requires a.Length >= 1. The precondition `a.Length > -1` is too weak and allows an empty array. The counterexample has a.Length = 0 and i = 1, so the invariant fails on loop entry. The same i also feeds `sorted(a, 0, i)`, whose precondition needs i <= a.Length. The comment shows the intended precondition was that the length is greater than 0.

The constructor's precondition 'capacity > -1' admits capacity == 0. Valid() requires 'this.capacity > 0', so with capacity = 0 the constructor cannot establish its postcondition 'ensures Valid()'. The counterexample confirms this: capacity = 0 at the failing return. The precondition is too weak for the class invariant the constructor must establish.

Method get has no precondition `requires Valid();`, unlike getLFUKey and put. So on entry nothing is known about capacity or cacheMap: capacity may be non-positive, |cacheMap| may exceed capacity, and stored values or frequencies may be negative. This breaks two things. First, the assertion at line 80 (key in cacheMap ==> cacheMap[key].0 >= 0) cannot be proved. Second, at the return (line 95), every conjunct of the postcondition Valid() fails, as the counterexamples show (e.g. capacity = -2437). The body only increments the frequency of an existing key, which would preserve Valid() if it held initially, but the missing precondition gives the method nothing to bridge from.

The precondition 'requires a.Length > -1' is trivially true, so it allows an empty array (a.Length = 0). The access m := a[0] at line 88 is then out of range. Even without that access, the invariant 1 <= i <= a.Length could not hold on entry, and the existential postcondition could not be satisfied for an empty array. The precondition is too weak to establish the loop's starting state.

queryFast's precondition allows j up to a.Length + 1, which is c.Length. Its postcondition calls sum(a, i, j), and sum requires j <= a.Length, so that postcondition is not well-formed. The call aux(a, c, i, j) also requires j <= a.Length. The counterexamples show j = a.Length + 1. The bound is off by one: indices into c run to a.Length, but sums over a may only use j <= a.Length.

The precondition `1<=x< (a.Length) + 1` allows x == a.Length, which the counterexample uses (x = a.Length = 6136). In that case the second loop never runs, since i := x already equals a.Length. Execution then reaches `p := a.Length-1`, so p == x-1 and the postcondition `x<=p<a.Length` fails. With x == a.Length no index p can satisfy x<=p<a.Length, so the method cannot meet its contract. The precondition is too weak: x must be strictly less than a.Length. With that bound, every return path gives x<=p<a.Length: either p := i with x<=i<a.Length, or p := a.Length-1 >= x.

The method only requires a.Length != 0 and puts no bound on x. When x == 0, the first loop starts with i == 1, so the invariant 0<=i<=x fails on entry (line 13). When x > a.Length, the quantifiers over 0<=j<i<=x in the invariants at lines 14-15 index a out of range. The ensures at line 17 also indexes a out of range. The second loop's invariant x<=i<=a.Length (line 25) cannot hold on entry because i := x exceeds a.Length. The counterexamples show exactly these cases: x = 0, and x larger than a.Length. The missing precondition is that x is a valid index of a and at least 1. That keeps 1 <= x so i starts within bounds, and x < a.Length so all array accesses are in range.

The row-sortedness precondition bounds j' by a.Length1 - 1, so it says nothing about the last column. The search starts at n = a.Length1-1. When a[m,n] < key the body increments m. Justifying that step requires every a[m,j] with j <= n to be <= a[m,n] < key, so that key is not in row m. Because the precondition excludes column a.Length1-1, Dafny cannot show the key is absent from row m. The existence invariant (line 11) is therefore not maintained. Without it, Dafny also cannot show m+1 < a.Length0, so the bounds invariant (line 10) fails to be preserved as well.

mroot3's precondition `n>=-1` admits n = -1. On loop entry r = 0 and y = n+1 = 0, so the invariant conjunct r*r<=n becomes 0 <= -1, which is false (column 24 of line 42). This also contradicts y>=r+1. The postcondition r*r <= n cannot hold for any r >= 0 when n is negative, so the precondition is too weak. It should match mroot1 and mroot2 and require n to be non-negative.

mroot2 has no precondition, so n may be negative (counterexample n = -10391). After r := n, the loop invariant 0<=r<=n && n<(r+1)*(r+1) fails at loop entry: 0<=r is false when r = n < 0. The postcondition also cannot hold for negative n, because no r>=0 satisfies r*r <= n. Every other mroot variant requires n>=0, and mroot2 omits it.

mmaxvalue1 has the precondition 'requires v.Length>-1', which allows an empty array (v.Length == 0). It then calls mmaximum1(v), whose precondition is 'requires v.Length>0'. That precondition cannot be proved at the call site, as the counterexample v.Length = 0 shows. With an empty array, 'm in v[..]' could not hold anyway. The caller's precondition is too weak.

The third precondition of binarySearchRec only says that elements before c are at most elem + 1. It should say they are at most elem. In the base case c == f+1 the method returns p := c-1, so the first postcondition needs v[u] <= elem for every u < c. The weakened precondition only gives v[u] <= elem + 1, so the postcondition does not follow. The counterexample shows this: c = 1, v[0] = 2329, elem = 2328 satisfies the weak precondition, but p = 0 violates v[0] <= elem. Recursive calls preserve the stronger property, since v[m] <= elem and sortedness give v[k] <= elem for all k <= m. Restoring the precondition therefore makes both the base case and the recursive cases verify.

The predicate sorted_seg has no precondition, so Dafny cannot show its body is well-formed. Nothing guarantees that the bounds i and j lie within the array. The quantifier ranges over i <= l <= k < j and indexes a[l] and a[k]. With i negative or j > a.Length, these accesses can be out of range, which is what the counterexamples show (i = -39, j = 7681; and a.Length = 2438 with j = 7681). Both reported errors are these index well-formedness failures at line 4. Every call site in both methods already passes bounds satisfying 0 <= i <= j <= a.Length (for example (c,i), (j,f), (i,f) and (c,i+1) with i < f), so adding this as the predicate's requires makes the body well-defined and keeps all uses valid.

The predicate sorted_seg has the precondition 0 <= i <= j <= a.Length + 1. This allows j == a.Length + 1. Inside the body, the quantifier ranges over k < j, so k (and l) can equal a.Length. The reads a[l] and a[k] at line 5 are then not provably in bounds, and the predicate's body is not well-formed. The counterexample shows exactly this: a.Length = 0 with j = 1, and a.Length = 39 with j = 40. The precondition is too weak to establish safe indexing. The intended bound for an exclusive end index is j <= a.Length.

The two errors (columns 41 and 49 of line 6) are well-formedness failures for the array reads a[l] and a[k] in the body of sorted_seg. The predicate's precondition `0 <= i <= j+1 <= (a.Length) + 1` allows j == a.Length. In that case k (and l) can equal a.Length, which is past the end of the array. The counterexamples show this: a.Length = 0 with j = 0, and a.Length = 1 with j = 1. The +1 on the upper bound is an off-by-one: j is an inclusive index, so it must be at most a.Length-1. Tightening the bound to j+1 <= a.Length makes the body well-formed. All call sites still satisfy the tighter bound: sorted_seg(a,0,a.Length-1), sorted_seg(a,0,i-1) with i <= a.Length, sorted_seg(a,0,j-1) with j <= i, and sorted_seg(a,j+1,i) inside the outer loop where i < a.Length.

segMaxSum's precondition only says v.Length>0 and puts no bounds on i. The counterexamples show both failure modes. With i = -1, the invariant 0<=j<=i is false at loop entry when j = 0. With i >= v.Length, the expressions Sum(v,k,i+1), Sum(v,k,j+1) and SumMaxToRight(v,j,s) are applied outside their preconditions (j<=v.Length and i<v.Length), and v[j+1] can be indexed out of range. So the precondition cannot establish the loop invariants or make the specification well-formed. The sibling method segSumaMaxima2 already uses the needed precondition 0<=i<v.Length.

The precondition of LemmaAscendingSubsequence is off by one: `i <= (|q1|-|q2|) + 1` lets `i + |q2|` be `|q1| + 1`. The slice `q1[i..i+|q2|]` is then out of bounds, so the requires clause itself is not well-formed (the two errors at line 197; the counterexamples have i=2 with |q1|=1, and |q2|=2 with |q1|=1). Because the slice may be undefined, the requires gives no usable link between q2 and an in-range window of q1. So Ascending(q1) cannot be carried over to the ensures Ascending(q2), which is why the empty lemma body fails at line 200. Both call sites (offset 0 for qleft and offset |qleft|+1 for qright) already satisfy the tighter bound, so tightening it does not break the callers.

pred_repair: requires forall k:: k in NumbersInSequence(q) ==> k < i
pred_diagnosis: lemma_all_small has an empty body, so its postcondition must follow from its preconditions alone. Its only precondition says each q[k] is a member of NumbersInSequence(q). That is a tautology and says nothing relating the elements of q to i. So 'forall j :: 0 <= j < |q| ==> q[j] < i' cannot be proved: the counterexample has i = 0 and q[22] = 7719. The symmetric lemma_all_big works because it also requires 'forall k :: k in NumbersInSequence(q) ==> k > i'. lemma_all_small is missing the matching upper-bound precondition. PrimeMap uses {:autocontracts}, so every method implicitly requires and ensures the class invariant Valid(): every key i in database maps to true exactly when prime(i). InsertPrime unconditionally sets database[n] := true, but nothing requires n to be prime. For a non-prime n such as 4 (the counterexample), the new entry 4 -> true breaks Valid(), so the implicit postcondition Valid() fails at the end of InsertPrime. The method needs a precondition saying that n really is prime, which the comment 'insert an already known prime number' already intends.

Mult's precondition `requires x >= -1 && y >= 0` is too weak. It admits x = -1, which matches the counterexample (x = -1, y = 7719). In that case the x == 0 branch is not taken. The else branch then asserts `x-1 >= 0`, but x-1 = -2, so the assertion at line 155 fails. The recursive call Mult(x-1, y) would also violate the callee's precondition, and the `decreases x` measure would no longer be bounded below by 0. The intended precondition is a non-negative x, so that the recursion counts down to the base case x == 0.

The precondition `requires |s1| <= (data.Length) + 1` is off by one: it allows |s1| == data.Length + 1. Every counterexample has exactly this shape. In that case the second requires indexes data[data.Length-1-i] with i = |s1|-1 = data.Length, so the index is -1 and the clause is ill-formed (line 75). For the same reason, the loop body's access data[data.Length - n1 + n] starts at index -1, so the in-body asserts relating data to s1 index out of range (lines 90, 93, 95). The post-loop assertion `|s1| <= data.Length` (line 105) also cannot be proved. The precondition is too weak to establish the in-range facts that the loop and its invariants rely on from the first iteration.

LinearSearch3 has no precondition relating |s1| to data.Length. Its only requires clause indexes data[data.Length-1-i] for every 0 <= i < |s1|, which is ill-formed when |s1| > data.Length (counterexample: data.Length = 36, |s1| = 39), so line 74 fails. LinearSearch2 has the bound, but it was omitted here. The other errors follow from the same gap. The invariant at line 86 and the loop guard expression data[data.Length - n1 + n] index data at positions that may be negative when n1 = |s1| > data.Length. The later assertions also rely on |s1| <= data.Length. One of them asserts it directly at line 92, and others index data[data.Length - n1]. So the precondition does not establish a well-defined context for the loop invariants and body accesses at loop entry.

In RotateLeft the precondition `requires a.Length > -1` is too weak because it admits an empty array (a.Length == 0). Two checks then fail. First, the postcondition `a[a.Length-1] == old(a[0])` indexes a[-1] and old(a[0]) out of range, so it is not well-formed. Second, at loop entry n = 0 and a.Length - 1 = -1, so the invariant `0 <= n <= a.Length - 1` cannot be established; `a[n] == old(a[0])` is also out of bounds. The counterexample (a.Length = 0, n = 0) shows exactly this. The intended precondition, used in the original completion and in RotateRight, is a non-empty array.

RotateRight has no precondition requiring a non-empty array, although the original intent (and RotateLeft) has `requires a.Length > 0`. When a.Length == 0, two things fail. First, the postcondition `a[0] == old(a[a.Length-1])` indexes out of range, so it is not well-formed. Second, the loop starts with n = 1, so the invariant `1 <= n <= a.Length` is false at loop entry (1 <= 0 does not hold). The counterexample a.Length = 0, n = 1 shows both failures. The fix is a missing precondition, not a wrong invariant.

UpWhileNotEqual has no precondition. Its loop invariant 0 <= i <= N cannot be established on entry when N is negative. The counterexample shows this: N = -1, so after i := 0 the conjunct i <= N is false. The other methods in the program include requires 0 <= N, and this one is missing it, so the invariant (and termination via N - i) is not established at loop entry.

Without sortedness, learning a[k+c] < x says nothing about a[k..k+c), and learning a[k+c] >= x says nothing about a[k+c+1..). So the loop's facts about which part is below x and which part is at or above x cannot be re-established after each step. The verifier reports the loop invariants as not maintained. The counterexample states also do not match the stated preconditions (for example, n+1 = 8308 is not a power of 2), so it is only a rough hint. Line 214 is the class OddList's override of method at. In the trait OddListSpec, at has the precondition `requires 0 <= index < (|s|) + 1`, which allows index == |s|. The class override instead requires `0 <= index < |s|`, which is a stronger precondition. Dafny checks that an overriding method's precondition is implied by the trait's precondition, and here it is not. The class precondition is also the one the implementation needs, because it returns s[index] and ensures s[index] == x, so index must be a valid position. The trait's precondition is the faulty line.

CircularLinkedList.removeAtIndex leaves out the `requires Valid()` precondition that the trait's spec declares. Without it, |l| may exceed capacity on entry. The counterexample has capacity = 1 and |l| = 3; removing one element gives |l| = 2 > capacity. So the postcondition `ensures Valid()` (0 <= |l| <= capacity) cannot be proved from the method's preconditions and body.

Sqare2 has the precondition a >= 0, which is weaker than the a >= 1 used in Sqare. Its loop starts with y := 1 and needs the invariant 1 <= y <= a, and the first assertion checks 1 <= 1 <= a. The counterexample a = 0 satisfies the precondition but makes 1 <= a false, so the invariant cannot be established at loop entry.

ComputeFact2 has no precondition, so n may be negative (the counterexample uses n = -1). Two checks fail as a result. First, the postcondition f == factorial(n) calls factorial outside its own precondition n >= 0, so the spec is not well-formed. Second, with x := 0 and n = -1, the invariant 0 <= x <= n is false on loop entry, which is the initiation failure. The missing requires clause is the root cause of both errors.

Init's precondition 'requires c > -1' allows c == 0. With c == 0, capacity is set to 0, but Valid() requires capacity > 0. The postcondition 'ensures Valid() && ...' therefore cannot be proved for c == 0, which is exactly the counterexample (c = 0, capacity = 0). The precondition is too weak to support the postcondition.

Push only requires Valid(), which allows the stack to be full (top == capacity - 1). The body then sets top := top + 1 and writes arr[top]. When the stack is full, the new top equals arr.Length, so the array write at line 71 is out of range. The counterexample shows this: capacity = 1 and top = 0 on entry, so top becomes 1. Push needs a precondition saying the stack is not full. The later postcondition Valid() (top < capacity) also depends on this.

The quantifier `forall i, j :: start <= i <= j < end ==> arr[i] <= arr[j]` indexes `arr[i]` and `arr[j]` (columns 48 and 58). RowColumnProduct's precondition was weakened to 'column < (m2.Length1) + 1', which allows column == m2.Length1. Its body calls RowColumnProductFrom, which requires 'column < m2.Length1', so that call's precondition cannot be proved when column == m2.Length1 (counterexample: column = 1236 = m2.Length1). The off-by-one bound in the requires clause is the cause.

The error at line 26 is the outer loop invariant `i <= a.Length`, which cannot be proved on entry. The loop starts with `i := 1`, but the precondition `a.Length > -1` is trivially true and allows an empty array. With a.Length == 0 and i == 1 (the counterexample), the invariant is false before the first iteration. It would also make `sorted(a, 0, i)` ill-formed. The precondition is too weak to establish the invariant at loop entry; it must guarantee the array is non-empty.

The error at line 27 is the loop invariant 'i <= a.Length', which cannot be established on entry. The loop counter is initialized to i := 1, but the precondition 'requires a.Length > -1' admits empty arrays. The counterexample has a.Length = 0 and i = 1, where i <= a.Length is false before the first iteration. Without that invariant, 'sorted_between(a, 0, i)' is also not well-formed, since it needs to <= a.Length. The precondition is too weak to establish the outer loop invariant at initiation.

SkipHead has no precondition: its `requires Valid()` clause is missing. Without it, nothing links `next` to `List` or `Repr`. Dafny therefore cannot show that r == null implies |List| == 1. When r != null, it also cannot show r.Valid(), r.List == List[1..], or r.Repr <= Repr. Every conjunct of Valid() (this in Repr, next in Repr, next.Repr <= Repr, this !in next.Repr, and so on) is unknown at the return point. The body `r := next` is correct, but the postcondition does not follow because the object is not assumed to be a well-formed list node on entry.

pred_diagnosis: The range precondition was weakened to -1 <= a[i], which contradicts the intended range [0..a.Length-2] stated in the comment. Inside the main loop the body evaluates d[a[i]]. If a[i] can be -1 (the counterexample has a[3089] = -1), the index is negative and out of range for d. Every iteration needs 0 <= a[i] < d.Length to index d safely and to keep the loop invariants about d, so this index check in the loop body fails.

pred_repair: requires exists p,q :: p != q && IsDuplicate(a, p) && IsDuplicate(a, q);  // two distinct duplicates exist
pred_diagnosis: The precondition stating that the array contains two distinct duplicated values is missing. The loop is `while (true)` and exits only by `return` once a second distinct duplicate is found. Its invariant `0 <= i < a.Length` (together with the related invariants about d) can only be maintained if the loop always reaches that return before i runs past the end of the array. Without a hypothesis guaranteeing two distinct duplicates, the verifier cannot rule out an iteration where i + 1 == a.Length and no second duplicate has been seen. So the loop invariant cannot be shown to be maintained. The original competition specification lists this fact as an explicit precondition, and it was dropped here.

FIND's precondition only says 0 <= f < N. It never relates N to A.Length, so A could be shorter than N. Every expression A[p], A[q], A[f] or A[g] with an index below N may then be out of range. This breaks well-formedness of the ensures clause (line 50), of the outer loop invariants at loop entry (lines 55-56), and of the read A[f] at line 58. The counterexamples all have A.Length < N, e.g. A.Length = 0 with N = 1. The original Hoare FIND requires N to equal the array length; without that, the precondition cannot establish well-defined invariants when the loop is entered.

The precondition of Lemma_Split was weakened to 'u <= |a| + 1'. Its ensures clause calls Count(a, t, u, x) and Count(a, s, u, x), which require 'u <= |a|'. With u = |a| + 1 these calls are outside Count's domain, so the lemma's postcondition is not well-formed and Dafny reports the function precondition failures at line 172. The counterexamples confirm this, with u = 1238 and |a| = 1237. The weakened requires does not guarantee what the specification needs.

Method Client has no precondition. At line 75 it builds the iterator with `new M(l, c)`, and M requires `l.Valid()`. With no `requires` clause on Client, nothing about `l` is known at that call. The counterexample shows invalid states, e.g. n = 2 with a.Length = 1, so all four conjuncts of Valid() fail. Because the iterator is created before the loop, its initial state is never established. The loop invariants `iter.Valid()` and `iter.xs <= l.Contents` therefore cannot start out justified either. The original program requires the list to be valid on entry to Client, and Main satisfies this through its loop invariant `myList.Valid()`.

The lemma crash_safe_single_tx only requires countdown >= -1. Its first statement calls init_ghost_state(init_log, init_mem, countdown), whose precondition is countdown >= 0 (line 40). With countdown = -1, as in the counterexample, that call precondition cannot be proved at line 504. As a result, the ghost state that the loop invariants (ghost_state_inv, ghost_tx_inv) rely on is never validly set up. The lemma's precondition is weaker than its callee needs: it should require countdown >= 0, which matches ghost_state_inv's s.countdown >= 0. The 'recover' entry in the output is a time-out, not this precondition failure.

Lemma bits_trim_front has the precondition `requires n > -1`. Since n is a nat, this is always true, so it rules nothing out. When n == 0, bits(0) == [], and the slice bits(n)[1..] in the ensures clause is out of range. That makes the postcondition ill-formed (error at col 27). It also cannot be proved, which is the second error at the lemma body. The counterexample n = 0 confirms this. The precondition was meant to exclude n == 0, so that bits(n) is non-empty and dropping its lowest bit gives n/2.

The precondition only constrains x1 (1 <= x1) and says nothing about x2. The outer loop invariant 1 <= y1 && 1 <= y2 needs y2 == x2 >= 1 at loop entry. With x1 = 1 and x2 = 0, the invariant fails on entry. The precondition is too weak: it should also require 1 <= x2.

Ghost method Lemma1 has no precondition on k. This causes two failures. First, its postcondition calls SumEmUp(0, k) and GSum(k), which both require 0 <= k, so the ensures clause is not well-formed (counterexample k = -1). Second, the loop invariant i <= k cannot be established on entry when i = 0 and k is negative (counterexample k = -2). Every other lemma in the class states 0 <= k or 0 <= n as a precondition; Lemma1 omits it.

The invariant `d <= r` on line 37 need not hold on loop entry. Before the loop r == n, and the precondition only gives n >= 0 && d > 0. With the counterexample n = 0, d = 1, r = 0, so d <= r is false before the first iteration. The invariant is also wrong in intent: the loop exits exactly when r < d, so the bound that holds throughout (and is needed for 0 <= r in the postcondition) is a lower bound of 0 on r, not d.

The function gcd has only the precondition m > 0 and nothing constrains n. In the counterexample m = 1, n = 0, the branch m > n calls gcd(m - n, n), which is gcd(1, 0) again. The arguments never shrink, so the termination measure on the recursive calls (around line 55) does not decrease and the function cannot be proved to terminate. Both arguments must be positive for each subtraction step to strictly decrease m + n. The intended use in gcdI already assumes n > 0, so the function's precondition is simply too weak.

The error is a well-formedness failure inside the body of predicate `partitioned` (the `a[k, 1]` / `a[k', 1]` accesses). Unlike `sorted`, `partitioned` has no precondition on the second dimension of the array. The counterexample has a.Length1 = 1, where column index 1 is out of range, so Dafny cannot prove that `a[k, 1]` is a valid index.
